concepts.title: The marketing environment framework
concepts.explain: Firms analyse their marketing environment using a framework with the consumer at the centre — anything that affects consumers affects marketers. Around the consumer is the microenvironment (the company's capabilities, competition and corporate partners) and the macroenvironment (culture, demographics, social trends, technology, economic situation and political/legal environment — CDSTEP). Firms must continuously monitor internal and external environments and be proactive, not reactive, adapting their offerings and marketing mix to new challenges and opportunities.
concepts.alt: Picture rings around a bullseye: the customer is the bullseye, the firm's immediate world (itself, rivals, partners) is the next ring, and the big forces (CDSTEP) are the outer ring pushing on everything inside.

terms.def: Factors close to the firm: company capabilities, competition, corporate partners.
Broad external factors: culture, demographics, social trends, technology, economy, political/legal (CDSTEP).
Anticipating environmental changes rather than responding after they happen.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Huron Canvas had to change its promotion when cotton canvas became scarce — showing why firms must monitor the environment.

concepts.title: Company capabilities & core competencies
concepts.explain: The first microenvironmental factor is the firm itself. Company capabilities — knowledge, facilities, patents, technology, people, financial resources — form core competencies. Successful firms focus on satisfying customer needs that match their core competencies, and can leverage those competencies into new products.
concepts.alt: Core competencies are a firm's superpowers; good marketing points them at customer needs the firm can actually solve.

terms.def: The firm's resources and strengths — knowledge, facilities, patents, technology, people, finances.
What the firm does exceptionally well, applied to satisfying customer needs.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Apple's competencies — product design, patents, software engineers, strong brand, supplier relationships and its ecosystem — let it move from Macs into the iPod, iPhone and iPad.

concepts.title: Competition — direct vs indirect
concepts.explain: Competition significantly affects the microenvironment. Direct competitors offer similar products in the same market (Apple and Samsung). Indirect competitors sell different products but compete for the same share of the customer's wallet (Starbucks vs Booster Juice, McDonald's, at-home coffee, Red Bull). Marketers must know competitors' strengths, weaknesses and likely reactions, and ask: should we compete, where, and how?
concepts.alt: Direct competitors are runners in your lane; indirect competitors are runners in other lanes chasing the same prize — the customer's money.

terms.def: Firms offering similar products/services in the same market.
Firms selling different products but aiming for the same share of the customer's wallet.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Bulldog Skincare found a niche in natural men's grooming while Gillette and Schick battled each other — and missed start-ups like Dollar Shave Club.

concepts.title: Competitive intelligence (CI)
concepts.explain: Competitive intelligence (CI) is used to collect and synthesise information about a firm's position relative to its rivals. It helps a firm plan how to beat competitors — improve where rivals fail, undercut prices, learn their target markets, or apply what works for others. Sources include strategic plans, the Canadian business database and web analytics. Some CI (like insider information) is a grey area legally, so firms often have employees sign non-disclosure agreements.
concepts.alt: CI is a firm's scouting report on the other team — legal scouting only, which is why employees sign NDAs.

terms.def: Collecting and synthesising information about the firm's position with respect to its rivals.
A confidentiality agreement limiting what information employees can share.

concepts.example: Illustrative: a café tracks a rival chain's menu prices and promotions on social media to decide its own seasonal specials.

concepts.title: Corporate partners
concepts.explain: Few firms work in isolation. Corporate partners — suppliers, other manufacturers, part makers, unions, transport companies, dealerships — work with the focal firm to create a seamless system that delivers goods and services when and where customers want them.
concepts.alt: A firm is one link in a chain; its corporate partners are the other links that get the product into the customer's hands.

terms.def: Parties that work with the focal firm (suppliers, manufacturers, distributors, dealers).

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Ford works with partners such as Harman Kardon, Goodyear, Michelin, Shell and its dealerships; Nau partners to make socially responsible apparel; Walmart's success is linked to supplier relationships.

concepts.title: Macroenvironmental factors — CDSTEP
concepts.explain: Marketers must understand macroenvironmental factors in the external environment, remembered by the acronym CDSTEP: Culture, Demographics, Social trends (social/natural trends), Technological advances, Economic situation, and Political/legal environment. These broad forces affect consumers and therefore the firm's marketing strategy.
concepts.alt: CDSTEP is a checklist of the "weather systems" of the market — big forces the firm can't control but must prepare for.

terms.def: Culture, Demographics, Social trends, Technological advances, Economic situation, Political/legal environment.

concepts.example: Illustrative: an EV maker watches CDSTEP — green social trends, battery technology, interest rates and government rebates all shape demand.

concepts.title: Culture — country culture & regional subcultures
concepts.explain: Culture is the shared meanings, beliefs, morals, values and customs of a group of people, transmitted by words, literature and institutions and passed down over generations. Country culture defines a nation as a whole (Canada vs Japan). Regional subcultures are distinct groups within a nation with their own values and customs (Ontario vs Quebec). Firms may need different approaches for different cultures — or bridge the gap with similar advertising across countries.
concepts.alt: Country culture is the national "personality"; regional subcultures are its local accents.

terms.def: Shared meanings, beliefs, morals, values and customs of a group of people.
Shared meanings, beliefs, values and customs that define a nation as a whole.
A distinct group within a nation with its own cultural values and customs.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Coca-Cola uses near-identical ads in English- and Spanish-speaking markets; Quebec residents are less likely than Ontarians to buy hot prepared meals.

concepts.title: Demographics
concepts.explain: Demographics are the characteristics of human populations and segments, especially those used to identify consumer markets — such as age, gender, income, education, race/ethnicity and population density. Demographic segmentation is the most common form because the information is so widely available. Firms use demographics to assess customers' needs and position themselves to deliver better value.
concepts.alt: Demographics are the population's "stats sheet" — the measurable facts marketers can look up.

terms.def: Characteristics of human populations and segments used to identify consumer markets.

concepts.example: Illustrative: a retirement-living company targets Canadians aged 65+ using census age data.

concepts.title: Generational cohorts
concepts.explain: A generational cohort is a group of people of the same generation who have similar purchase behaviours because of shared experiences and stage of life — affecting social media use, fashion, benefits sought, values and views of work. The slide table lists Generation Z (born after 1997), Generation Y/Millennials (1981–1996), Generation X (1965–1980) and Baby Boomers (1946–1964), plus Seniors. Marketers position products differently depending on the cohort they target.
concepts.alt: Cohorts are like graduating classes of society — people who "grew up together" through the same events tend to buy alike.

terms.def: A group of the same generation with similar purchase behaviours due to shared experiences and life stage.
Born after 1997 (slide table) — digital natives.
Millennials, born 1981–1996 (slide table).
Born 1965–1980 (slide table).

concepts.example: Illustrative: a streaming service promotes short vertical clips to Gen Z and nostalgic classics to Boomers.

concepts.title: Income
concepts.explain: Purchasing power is tied to income, which Statistics Canada tracks. Many middle-class families have felt a decline in purchasing power because costs like health care, taxes and tuition have risen faster than incomes. The slides cite median after-tax family income of $68,400, and the top 10% earning over $226,000. Canadians are commonly grouped into upper, middle and working/low income classes — income classes, not fixed social classes, because education and income enable mobility. The middle class can afford a good life most of the time but is careful and value-conscious. Consumers are searching for value more than in previous decades.
concepts.alt: Income sets the size of the shopping basket; when costs rise faster than pay, people fill it more carefully — hunting for value.

terms.def: The ability to buy, tied to income.
Upper, middle and working/low income groups (mobile, not fixed social classes).
Can afford a good life most of the time; careful, value-conscious spenders.

concepts.example: Illustrative: discount grocers like No Frills appeal to value-seeking middle- and lower-income shoppers.

concepts.title: Education
concepts.explain: Higher education is strongly linked to better jobs and higher incomes, which determine spending power; degree holders earn significantly more on average, and Canada is highly educated. Marketers combine education with occupation and income to better predict buying behaviour, segmenting beyond income alone and targeting education-based preferences.
concepts.alt: Education is an early clue to future income — and combined with job and pay, it sharpens predictions of what people buy.

terms.def: Level of schooling, linked to income and therefore spending power.

concepts.example: Illustrative: a premium business-news subscription targets university-educated professionals.

concepts.title: Gender
concepts.explain: Gender roles are blurring, pushing firms to design and position products beyond traditional male–female boundaries and to focus on inclusivity and shared decision-making. Women are now decision makers, not just influencers: they outperform men in education, head more than 20% of Canadian households, and make the majority of household purchasing decisions.
concepts.alt: The old "pink aisle / blue aisle" map is outdated — marketers now design for whoever is actually deciding, and that's often women.

terms.def: Traditional male/female roles are less distinct, affecting product design and positioning.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): RONA+ redesigned stores with brighter spaces and open floor plans that appeal to female DIYers; Bandai Namco's mixed-gender gaming tournament.

concepts.title: Ethnicity
concepts.explain: Canada's ethnic composition is changing. About 23% of Canadians are foreign-born, and immigration has driven over 75% of population growth since 2016; by 2030 growth will be mainly from immigration. By 2036 visible minorities are expected to total about 15 million (nearly 39% of the population). South Asian and Chinese communities are the fastest-growing and affluent, and Indigenous peoples (5% of the population) grew 9.4% from 2016–2021. This is both a challenge (understanding each group's culture, values and spending) and an opportunity, so brands tailor products, signage and campaigns.
concepts.alt: Canada's customer base is becoming a mosaic; brands that learn each tile's colours can serve the whole picture.

terms.def: Ethnic composition of the population — a fast-changing demographic in Canada.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Sephora used an all-Indigenous cast for National Indigenous History Month; Harley-Davidson created the Tough Turban for Sikh riders.

concepts.title: Technological advances
concepts.explain: Technology has impacted every aspect of marketing: new products (smartwatches), new forms of communication (Zoom, Instagram) and new retail channels (Amazon, Temu, Shein). Constant mobile connectivity (Wi-Fi, 5G, smartphones, wearables) enables anytime shopping; near-field communication, payment apps and streaming personalise experiences; AI, robotics and the Internet of Things transform how firms collect data and interact with customers; and mobile tools strengthen loyalty through convenience and customisation.
concepts.alt: Technology keeps rewriting the rules of the game board — new pieces (products), new ways to talk (channels) and new places to play (stores).

terms.def: Macro factor — new technologies creating new products, communication and retail channels.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Netflix uses technology to recommend and even develop content; Coca-Cola Freestyle machines use AI and big data to predict new flavours.

concepts.title: Artificial intelligence
concepts.explain: AI enables machines and software to learn from data and perform tasks that once required human decision-making — speech recognition, translation, transcription. Marketers use AI for personalisation, automation, chatbots and faster content creation, and primarily for advanced customer segmentation (CRM and big data), media selection and buying, and customer engagement. AI supports both consumer convenience and business efficiency.
concepts.alt: AI is a tireless assistant that studies everything customers do and suggests the next best move.

terms.def: Computer systems that learn from data and perform tasks requiring human intelligence.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Wealthsimple's chatbot handles ~70% of customer inquiries; Stitch Fix blends AI with human stylists; The North Face's Expert Personal Shopper asks questions to suggest items.

concepts.title: Robotics
concepts.explain: Robotics now handle tasks across retail, warehouses, farms and health care, improving speed, safety and labour efficiency. Service robots cut labour costs and increase throughput, and retailers test autonomous drones for faster, cheaper last-mile delivery.
concepts.alt: Robots take over repetitive or dangerous jobs so products move faster and cheaper — the assembly line went mobile.

terms.def: Machines performing tasks in retail, warehouses, farms and health care to improve speed, safety and efficiency.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Amazon uses warehouse robots and FAA-approved delivery drones; some restaurant robots produce up to 80 pizzas per hour.

concepts.title: Internet of Things
concepts.explain: The Internet of Things (IoT) links multiple smart, sensor-enabled devices to collect and share data — for example homes that switch to eco mode during high-consumption times. Smart vehicles and home systems use sensors to predict maintenance needs, and retailers use IoT data to optimise inventory, fix pricing errors and monitor operations. Connected devices automate homes while giving firms insights to improve service, supply and customer experience.
concepts.alt: IoT turns everyday objects into chatty teammates — your fridge, thermostat and car all "talk" and share data.

terms.def: Network of smart, sensor-enabled devices that collect and share data.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): iRobot, Samsung and Nest connect appliances to apps for automation and remote control.

concepts.title: Economic situation
concepts.explain: Marketers monitor the economy at home and abroad because it affects how consumers buy and spend. Key factors: inflation (erodes purchasing power; the target is ~2%, and higher inflation pushes consumers toward lower prices and better value), interest rates (the cost of borrowing money, affecting borrowing and spending — high household debt limits discretionary purchases), foreign currency exchange rates (a weak Canadian dollar boosts tourism and exports but raises import costs), and recession (negative economic growth for at least two consecutive quarters, shifting spending toward essentials and low-cost luxuries).
concepts.alt: The economy is the tide — when it goes out (inflation, high rates, recession), every boat (consumer budget) sinks a little and people spend more cautiously.

terms.def: The general rate of price increases; erodes purchasing power.
The cost of borrowing money.
The value of one currency relative to another.
A period of negative economic growth for at least two consecutive quarters.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): a weaker Canadian dollar attracts foreign shoppers and tourists, boosting Canadian retail.

concepts.title: Political/legal environment
concepts.explain: The political/legal environment includes government policies, laws and regulations that shape how firms compete and market products. Competition and fair-trade laws prevent monopolies, misleading advertising and unsafe products to protect consumers. Industry regulations can restrict or enable markets (deregulation, safety mandates, environmental rules, taxes). Compliance raises costs and paperwork but can create opportunities (demand for car seats, hands-free devices, eco-friendly products). Examples of legislation: Competition Act, Consumer Packaging and Labelling Act, PIPEDA, Food and Drugs Act.
concepts.alt: Laws are the rulebook of the game — they can block some plays, but new rules also open new moves (like car-seat laws creating a market).

terms.def: Government policies, laws and regulations that promote or inhibit trade and marketing.
Canadian law protecting fair competition (listed on slide 41).
Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act — privacy legislation.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): safety mandates created demand for child car seats and hands-free devices.

concepts.title: Social & natural trends; UN Sustainable Development Goals
concepts.explain: Social and natural trends shape consumer values in Canada and around the world. They change in popularity over time, so marketers work to identify emerging trends and judge whether they are opportunities or threats. A historic agreement of 193 world leaders produced the 17 Global Goals of Sustainable Development, highlighting social issues such as food, clean water, health care and sanitation, mainly by eliminating extreme poverty. Trends covered: greener consumers, privacy, time-poor society, efficient food distribution, and health and wellness.
concepts.alt: Social trends are society's changing mood board — marketers watch it to see what customers will care about next.

terms.def: Shifts in values and concerns (e.g., sustainability, privacy, wellness) that shape consumer behaviour.
17 global goals agreed by 193 world leaders addressing basic needs and poverty.

concepts.example: Illustrative: a clothing brand aligns its sustainability report with the UN goals to appeal to socially conscious buyers.

concepts.title: Greener consumers & green marketing
concepts.explain: Green marketing is a strategic effort by firms to supply customers with environmentally friendly merchandise. Over 90% of Canadians believe individuals can reduce pollution, over half of households recycle, and 69% of consumers say they'd pay a premium for products that benefit society or the environment — yet Canadians generate 694 kg of waste per person and only 9% of plastic is recycled. Green demand drives energy-efficient appliances, organic goods and recycled products, but stricter laws now require proof of claims to prevent greenwashing.
concepts.alt: Green marketing sells "doing good" — but customers and regulators now ask for receipts, so empty eco-claims (greenwashing) backfire.

terms.def: A strategic effort by firms to supply customers with environmentally friendly merchandise.
Making environmental claims without proof (now restricted by stricter laws).

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Patagonia's 'Don't buy this jacket' and refurbished clothing; LEGO's 'Rebuild the World'; Natasha Tonić's hemp swimwear.

concepts.title: Privacy concerns
concepts.explain: Consumers increasingly sense a loss of privacy: 80% globally want more control over how companies use their personal data, while risky habits persist (74% of Canadians sometimes reuse passwords). Tracking backlash and costly data breaches (average Canadian breach ~$6.75M) make privacy a serious issue, and firms must inform consumers how they protect privacy; governments have instituted new privacy rules.
concepts.alt: Data is valuable to firms, but customers want the keys to their own house — overstep, and trust (and lawsuits) follow.

terms.def: Consumers' worry about how firms collect and use their personal data.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): the Tim Hortons app collected location data even when not in use, leading to investigations and lawsuits.

concepts.title: Time-poor society
concepts.explain: With more time spent at work, time for home and leisure has shrunk. Time-poor consumers multitask to cope, and services that do tasks people no longer have time for — housecleaning, errands, cooking — have grown. Marketers must find creative ways to reach these consumers, often relying on technology to make life easier.
concepts.alt: When time is the scarcest resource, convenience becomes the product.

terms.def: Consumers with little leisure time who multitask and value convenience.

concepts.example: Illustrative: meal-kit and grocery-delivery services save busy households time on shopping and cooking.

concepts.title: Efficient food distribution & health and wellness
concepts.explain: Food trends drive major markets — organic products, portion-controlled snacks, calorie-tracking apps and meal kits. Food waste remains significant (Canadians waste about 79 kg per person), so firms use AI, apps and donation programs to reduce waste and link sustainability to marketing. Health and wellness concerns fuel a US$1.8 trillion wellness industry — biomonitoring tech, fitness apps, yoga and wellness services — while regulators push responsible food marketing, especially to children.
concepts.alt: People increasingly want food that's smart (less waste) and lives that are healthy — and they'll pay brands that help with both.

terms.def: Rising demand for fitness, mindfulness and tech tools to manage well-being.
Trend toward reducing waste across the food value chain.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Hellmann's food-waste initiatives and Unilever's 'Future Foods'; MyFitnessPal and Lose It calorie apps.

concepts.title: The consumer decision process
concepts.explain: The consumer decision process is the series of steps consumers go through before, during and after a purchase: (1) need recognition, (2) information search, (3) alternative evaluation, (4) purchase decision, and (5) postpurchase. Marketers break buying into these steps because it is hard to see how consumers decide as a whole; studying each step separately shows where marketing can influence the outcome.
concepts.alt: Think of it like planning a trip: you realise you need a break (need), look up destinations (search), compare a few options (evaluate), book one (purchase), then decide whether the trip was worth it (postpurchase).

terms.def: The steps consumers go through before, during and after making purchases.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): a meal-kit service like HelloFresh responds to a need busy households recognise — a good dinner without the shopping and prep.

concepts.title: Need recognition (functional vs psychological needs)
concepts.explain: Need recognition starts when a consumer notices a gap between their current state and a desired state (e.g., hungry → wanting food). Needs can be functional — about the performance or utility of a product — or psychological — about personal gratification such as status, emotions or self-image. Most products satisfy both, but one usually dominates. Marketers trigger needs through reminders, awareness campaigns, image appeals and product placement.
concepts.alt: A functional need asks "Will it do the job?"; a psychological need asks "How will it make me feel or look?" Plain bleach cleans clothes (functional); insisting on a particular brand because it feels better is psychological.

terms.def: Noticing a gap between your current state and a desired state.
Needs that pertain to the performance or utility of a product or service.
Needs that pertain to personal gratification — status, emotions, self-image.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): a Dior Minaudière clutch can satisfy a functional need (carrying items) but mostly satisfies psychological needs like prestige.

concepts.title: Information search (internal vs external)
concepts.explain: After recognising a need, consumers search for information to evaluate options and reduce uncertainty. An internal search uses the buyer's own memory and past experiences. An external search looks outside personal knowledge — friends, reviews, influencers and online sources. Search effort rises with the importance, cost or perceived risk of the purchase (a car versus a small everyday item). Marketers support search with information, reviews, guarantees and risk-reducing signals.
concepts.alt: Internal search is checking your own "mental notes"; external search is asking the world. Remembering that your last pair of Nikes lasted two years is internal; reading Reddit threads about running shoes is external.

terms.def: The buyer examines their own memory and knowledge about the product or service.
The buyer seeks information outside their personal knowledge base (friends, reviews, online).

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): consumers see an outfit on a celebrity, then look it up on social media and search engines to decide where to buy it.

concepts.title: Factors affecting search — benefits vs costs, locus of control
concepts.explain: How much consumers search depends on several factors. First, the perceived benefits of making a good decision versus the perceived costs of searching (is it worth the time and effort?). Second, locus of control: people with an internal locus of control believe they are in charge of their own outcomes, so they spend significantly more time and effort searching; people with an external locus of control believe fate or a higher power decides, so they search less. A third factor — perceived risk — is covered separately.
concepts.alt: Internal locus = "If I do my homework, I'll get the best deal." External locus = "Whatever happens, happens." The first person shops around; the second buys the first decent option.

terms.term: Perceived benefits vs perceived costs of search
terms.def: Whether the benefit of a good decision is worth the time/effort of searching.
Belief that you control outcomes — leads to more search effort.
Belief that fate/a higher power controls outcomes — leads to less search effort.

concepts.example: Illustrative: a student who compares ten student-bank accounts before choosing one shows an internal locus of control.

concepts.title: Perceived risk in purchase decisions
concepts.explain: Risk and risk perceptions affect how much consumers search, and can delay or discourage a purchase. Five types: performance risk (the product performs poorly), financial risk (the money spent, including costs of using it), psychological risk (how you'll feel if it doesn't convey the right image), social risk (fear others won't regard the purchase positively), and physiological risk (fear of actual physical harm if it doesn't perform properly).
concepts.alt: Ask five worried questions: Will it work? (performance) Will I waste money? (financial) Will I feel bad about myself? (psychological) Will others judge me? (social) Could it hurt me? (physiological)

terms.def: Perceived danger that the product or service performs poorly.
Risk tied to the monetary outlay, including initial cost and cost of use.
Risk about how you'll feel if the product doesn't convey the right image.
Fear that others won't regard the purchase positively.
Fear of actual physical harm if the product doesn't perform properly.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slide notes): choosing a gift for an office grab bag, your mother, or your future mother-in-law involves increasing psychological risk.

concepts.title: Alternative evaluation — retrieval & evoked sets
concepts.explain: In alternative evaluation consumers compare options, often while still searching. They don't consider every brand: the retrieval set is all the brands they can recall from memory, and the evoked set is the smaller group they seriously consider. Remembering a brand doesn't mean you'll consider it. Evaluations focus on evaluative criteria — important attributes such as price, quality, fit, features and brand reputation. Determinant attributes are features that matter to the buyer and on which competing brands are perceived to differ.
concepts.alt: The retrieval set is every restaurant you can name; the evoked set is the three you'd actually suggest for dinner tonight.

terms.def: Brands a consumer can readily bring forth from memory.
The brands a consumer seriously considers when making a purchase decision.
Important attributes used to compare alternative products.
Features important to the buyer on which competing brands are perceived to differ.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Macy's is in women's retrieval set for business apparel, but Banana Republic is in the evoked set for young women seeking business apparel.

concepts.title: Compensatory vs non-compensatory decision rules
concepts.explain: Consumer decision rules are criteria consumers use, consciously or not, to choose quickly among alternatives. A compensatory rule trades attributes off against each other, so good characteristics compensate for bad ones — e.g., weighting mileage, style, price and accessories and picking the highest overall score. A non-compensatory rule chooses on a subset of characteristics regardless of the others — one factor prevails and is non-negotiable (e.g., rejecting a car with great mileage simply because the price is too high).
concepts.alt: Compensatory is a weighted report card — a weak grade in one subject can be offset by strong grades elsewhere. Non-compensatory is a "must pass" rule — fail one required subject and you're out, no matter the rest.

terms.def: Consumer trades off characteristics so good ones compensate for bad ones (weighted scores).
Choice based on a subset of characteristics regardless of others; one factor prevails.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): in the weighted car table Toyota scores highest (8.2) overall, but using price alone (non-compensatory) Nissan wins.

concepts.title: Decision heuristics (mental shortcuts)
concepts.explain: Decision heuristics are mental shortcuts that help consumers narrow down choices. Price: buyers may assume a higher price means better quality ("you get what you pay for") or pick the middle-priced option as a safe compromise. Brand: buying familiar brand names reduces uncertainty and feels safer than generics. Product presentation: how a product is presented influences the decision. Marketers support evaluation by highlighting comparisons, unique features, samples or trials.
concepts.alt: Heuristics are like autocomplete for decisions — instead of reasoning through everything, your brain fills in "expensive = good" or "known brand = safe".

terms.def: Mental shortcuts that help consumers narrow down their choices.
Using price as a cue — higher price = better quality, or choosing the middle option.
Choosing familiar/national brands because they feel safer and higher quality.
How a product is presented influences the decision.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Lululemon's distinctive design and premium branding act as quick cues of quality, so shoppers choose without extensive comparison.

concepts.title: Purchase decision & conversion
concepts.explain: Purchase intentions don't always become purchases — the item may be unavailable or there may be another stumbling block. Retailers therefore track the conversion rate: how well they convert purchase intentions into purchases. Abandoned online carts signal lost sales, so retailers use reminders, low-stock alerts and limited-time offers to close the sale. Reducing friction — easy checkout, multiple payment options, fast delivery, being where the customer shops — plus personalisation and in-store support turns positive evaluations into completed purchases.
concepts.alt: The purchase step is the last metre of a race — lots of runners (shoppers) fall at the finish line if the checkout is slow or confusing. Conversion rate measures how many cross it.

terms.def: How well a retailer converts purchase intentions into purchases.
An online cart left without purchase — a signal of lost sales.

concepts.example: Illustrative: an online store emails 'You left something in your cart — only 2 left!' to recover abandoned carts.

concepts.title: Postpurchase — satisfaction, dissonance, loyalty
concepts.explain: Postpurchase is the final step. It has three possible outcomes: customer satisfaction (+), postpurchase dissonance (−) and customer loyalty (+). Satisfaction comes from meeting realistic expectations with consistent performance and service. Postpurchase dissonance (buyer's remorse) is the doubt or regret consumers feel after a high-cost or high-risk purchase. To ensure satisfaction marketers should: build realistic expectations (not too high, not too low); demonstrate correct product use; stand behind the product with money-back guarantees and warranties; encourage customer feedback; and periodically contact customers to thank them. Long-term success depends on turning first-time buyers into loyal customers.
concepts.alt: After buying, the story either ends happily (satisfied → loyal) or with second thoughts (dissonance). Marketers act like a good host after a party — checking in, explaining how things work, and offering to fix problems.

terms.def: Psychological discomfort/regret after a purchase, especially high-cost or high-risk (buyer's remorse).
Result of meeting realistic expectations with consistent performance and service.
Repeat purchasing and attachment that grows from satisfying experiences.

concepts.example: Illustrative: a car dealer calls a week after the sale to answer questions and remind the buyer of the warranty to reduce buyer's remorse.

concepts.title: Undesirable consumer behaviour & negative word-of-mouth
concepts.explain: Dissatisfied customers can behave in ways that hurt firms. Passive consumers simply stop buying or recommending, quietly reducing repeat sales. Negative word-of-mouth spreads complaints and dissatisfaction, often to many others — unhappy customers share bad experiences more readily than satisfied ones share good ones, and social media amplifies complaints instantly. Proactive customer service and open feedback channels help resolve issues and limit damage.
concepts.alt: A happy customer tells a friend; an unhappy one tells the whole group chat — and now the group chat is the internet.

terms.def: Customers spreading complaints/dissatisfaction to others.
A dissatisfied customer who quietly stops buying or recommending.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slide notes): Whirlpool keeps negative comments visible on its brand Facebook pages to open discussion and show how it fixes problems.

concepts.title: Factors influencing consumer buying decisions
concepts.explain: The decision process doesn't happen in a vacuum. Three groups of factors influence it: psychological factors (internal to the consumer — motives, attitudes, perception, learning, lifestyle), social factors (family, reference groups, culture), and situational factors (purchase situation, shopping situation, temporal state). Involvement also affects how the process plays out.
concepts.alt: Psychological = what's going on inside your head; social = the people around you; situational = the moment you're in.

terms.def: Influences internal to the consumer: motives, attitudes, perception, learning, lifestyle.
Family, reference groups and culture.
Purchase situation, shopping situation and temporal state.

concepts.example: Illustrative: choosing a university can be shaped by your motives (psychological), your parents' opinions (social), and an application deadline (situational).

concepts.title: Motives & Maslow's hierarchy of needs
concepts.explain: A motive is a need or want strong enough to drive behaviour and trigger action. Abraham Maslow's hierarchy explains five levels of needs: physiological (basics like food, drink, rest, shelter), safety (protection, health, secure employment), social/love (belonging, family), esteem (image, confidence, how others see us), and self-actualization (personal growth and values-based choices). Marketers convert these needs into wants by linking products to them.
concepts.alt: Picture a pyramid: you build from the base (food, shelter) up through safety, belonging and respect toward the top (becoming your best self). Ads pick a level and speak to it.

terms.def: A need or want strong enough to cause a person to seek satisfaction.
Basic biological necessities — food, drink, rest, shelter.
Protection and security — health, shelter, secure employment.
Belonging and relationships — family, friends.
Confidence, image and how others see us.
Personal growth and choices aligned with identity or beliefs.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): a Subway ad satisfies the physiological need for food while saying healthy eating can taste good.

concepts.title: Attitude (cognitive, affective, behavioural)
concepts.explain: An attitude is a learned, lasting evaluation that shapes how consumers think, feel and act toward a product or idea. It is usually positive or negative (rarely neutral). Attitudes have three components: cognitive (beliefs — "yoga is relaxing and makes me flexible"), affective (feelings — "yoga makes me feel calm"), and behavioural (actions — enrolling in a class, buying a mat). Ideally the three align; when they don't, it can lead to dissonance. Attitudes are slow to change but can be influenced through persuasive messages, experiences and positive interactions.
concepts.alt: Remember "Think – Feel – Do": what you believe (cognitive), how you feel (affective), and what you do (behavioural).

terms.def: A learned, lasting evaluation of a product or idea that shapes thinking, feeling and acting.
What we believe to be true.
What we feel — like or dislike.
The actions we take based on what we know and feel.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): believing yoga improves health (cognitive), feeling relaxed about it (affective), and regularly attending classes or buying gear (behavioural).

concepts.title: Perception & selective processes
concepts.explain: Perception is the process by which we select, organise and interpret information to form a meaningful picture of the world. It works through the senses (sight, smell, touch, sound, taste), and experiences and memories shape meaning — so the same brand can be viewed positively by one person and negatively by another. Consumers filter messages through selective exposure, selective attention, selective comprehension and selective retention. Marketers must design packaging, labelling, branding and communications that stand out and reinforce the intended message.
concepts.alt: Your brain is a bouncer: it decides which messages get in (exposure), which get noticed (attention), how they're understood (comprehension), and which are remembered (retention).

terms.def: The process by which we select, organise and interpret information to form a meaningful picture of the world.
Consumers choose which messages they're exposed to.
Consumers notice only some of the messages they're exposed to.
Consumers interpret messages in their own way.
Consumers remember only some of what they perceive.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): warm lighting, music, aroma and cozy design turn a simple coffee purchase into a premium 'third place' experience; Volvo is perceived as 'safe'.

concepts.title: Learning
concepts.explain: Learning is a change in a person's thought process or behaviour that arises from experience, and it takes place throughout the decision process. Information, trials and interactions shape what consumers believe and feel about brands. Positive experiences build habits, preferences and purchase intentions, and learning reinforces attitudes and perceptions — making repeat purchases more likely.
concepts.alt: Learning is the "lesson" a consumer takes from experience: every good (or bad) experience updates their mental rulebook for the next purchase.

terms.def: A change in thought process or behaviour that arises from experience.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): using the Tide Eco-Box teaches consumers that less packaging can still clean well, reinforcing repeat purchase.

concepts.title: Lifestyle
concepts.explain: Lifestyle reflects how consumers spend their time and money and how they want to live. Purchases often signal identity, not just function, aligning with real or aspirational lifestyles. Some products meet practical needs while others communicate image and self-expression. Brands succeed when they match customers' daily habits, values and personal goals.
concepts.alt: Lifestyle is the "story" of how someone lives — and many purchases are props that help tell that story.

terms.def: How consumers spend their time and money and how they want to live.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Tiffany jewellery signals a luxury, milestone-driven lifestyle for consumers who want purchases to reflect status and identity.

concepts.title: Social factor — family
concepts.explain: Many purchases involve the whole family, with members playing different roles — users, influencers and decision makers — at different steps (information search, evaluation, final choice). Children and teens increasingly shape household spending, even on big-ticket items like cars, travel and technology. Marketers often treat the family as one unit and must target the whole family, not just the primary buyer.
concepts.alt: A family purchase is a group project: one person researches, another has opinions, and someone signs the cheque.

terms.def: A family member who shapes the search/evaluation without making the final decision.
The family member who makes the final choice.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): a family car purchase where different members search, influence preferences and negotiate the final choice together.

concepts.title: Reference groups (membership, aspirational, dissociative)
concepts.explain: A reference group is any person or group consumers use as a benchmark for beliefs, feelings, behaviours and purchases. Membership groups are groups you currently belong to (your program, McMaster students, your gym). Aspirational groups are groups you aren't part of but want to join (sports teams, celebrities). Dissociative groups are groups you want to distance yourself from. Reference groups influence buying by offering information, rewarding approved behaviour and enhancing self-image; marketers target influential groups to spark adoption and social proof.
concepts.alt: Membership = "I'm one of them." Aspirational = "I want to be one of them." Dissociative = "I don't want to be seen as one of them."

terms.def: One or more persons used as a basis for comparison regarding beliefs, feelings and behaviours.
A group you currently belong to.
A group you are not part of but want to belong to.
A group you want to distance yourself from.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Birkenstocks signal an 'earthy', casual lifestyle, letting consumers align with the identity of their reference group.

concepts.title: Social factor — culture
concepts.explain: Culture shapes consumers' values, beliefs and behaviours, influencing what they buy and how they shop. Strategies must adapt across countries and within diverse subcultures (regional vs country culture). Consumers prefer brands that genuinely understand their cultural needs rather than superficial gestures, so retailers tailor products and assortments to local communities. Organisations (B2B) also have distinct cultures (e.g., people-focused, customer-centric).
concepts.alt: Culture is the "operating system" people grow up with — it decides which apps (products) feel natural to use.

terms.def: Shared values, beliefs and behaviours that shape what people buy and how they shop.
A distinct group within a nation with its own values and customs.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): stores like FreshCo and Adonis offer halal meats and culturally specific products to build trust with diverse shoppers.

concepts.title: Situational factors (purchase, shopping, temporal)
concepts.explain: Situational factors are specific to the situation and can override, or at least influence, psychological and social issues. Purchase situation: the reason or occasion for buying (a gift, a work event) changes what you buy. Shopping (sensory) situation: the store environment — lighting, displays, aroma, music, staff, customer service — influences the decision. Temporal state: time pressure and mood (a sale ending today, a deadline, a bad day) affect the purchase.
concepts.alt: Ask: WHY am I buying (purchase situation)? WHERE/what's the setting (shopping situation)? WHEN and in what mood (temporal state)?

terms.def: Factors specific to the situation that override or influence psychological and social issues.
The occasion/reason for the purchase (e.g., a gift) that changes what is bought.
The store environment — lighting, displays, aroma, music, staff.
Time pressure and mood at the time of purchase.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): budget-shopper Priya buys from Tiffany & Co. because it's her best friend's birthday (purchase), the store feels luxurious (sensory), and the sale ends today (temporal).

concepts.title: Involvement & the elaboration likelihood model
concepts.explain: Involvement is how much consumers care about a purchase, and it shapes the decision process. High-involvement purchases (expensive, risky, infrequent or expressive) involve extended problem solving and careful research. Low-involvement purchases rely on limited problem solving, habits or impulse. The elaboration likelihood model shows the same ad is processed deeply by highly involved consumers (more research, comparisons, strong attitudes) and superficially by less involved ones (ignored or weak attitudes).
concepts.alt: Involvement is the "care dial". Turned up, you read the fine print; turned down, you skim the headline — even if it's the very same ad.

terms.def: How much consumers care about a purchase.
The same message is processed deeply by involved consumers and superficially by uninvolved ones.

concepts.example: Illustrative: a first-time car buyer studies every spec in a review video, while someone casually scrolling barely notices the same ad.

concepts.title: Types of buying decisions
concepts.explain: Extended problem solving: high effort — reading reviews, researching and comparing — for expensive, risky or important purchases (car, house, laptop); common in fashion/apparel for expressive items. Limited problem solving: moderate effort, relying more on past experience than new information (clothing, a backpack). Impulse buying: spontaneous, little thought, often triggered by in-store cues at checkout. Habitual decision making: almost no conscious effort — consumers automatically repurchase familiar brands (milk, coffee); this needs the least time and effort.
concepts.alt: Effort ladder from top to bottom: extended (research mode) → limited (quick check) → impulse (spur of the moment) → habitual (autopilot).

terms.def: High time and effort to analyse alternatives; used when the decision entails a lot of risk.
Moderate effort; relies more on past experience than new information.
A spontaneous purchase with little thought, often triggered by in-store cues.
A purchase made with little conscious effort — autopilot repurchasing.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): buying a house is extended; grabbing a Coffee Crisp at checkout is impulse; your daily Tim Hortons coffee is habitual.

concepts.title: The STP process
concepts.explain: Segmentation, targeting and positioning (STP) is a five-step process. Segmentation: Step 1 establish overall strategy or objectives, Step 2 choose segmentation bases. Targeting: Step 3 evaluate segment attractiveness, Step 4 select the target market/targeting strategy. Positioning: Step 5 identify and develop a positioning strategy. Segmentation finds distinct groups with similar needs; targeting focuses resources on the most attractive segments the firm can serve best; positioning shapes how the brand is perceived relative to competitors in customers' minds.
concepts.alt: STP is like throwing a party: decide your goal (1), sort potential guests into groups (2), judge which groups are worth inviting (3), pick who to invite (4), then decide how to describe the party so they want to come (5).

terms.def: Dividing a market into distinct groups of customers with similar needs.
Evaluating segments and focusing resources on the most attractive ones the firm can serve.
How the brand is perceived in customers' minds relative to competitors.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Wild Lot Farm Distillery designs products for health-conscious drinkers, local-experience seekers and social-occasion buyers, positioned on 'real ingredients, natural flavours'.

concepts.title: Step 1 — establish overall strategy or objectives
concepts.explain: STP starts with the firm's mission and objectives, which guide who the firm should serve and what value it promises. A SWOT analysis clarifies internal strengths and weaknesses and external opportunities and threats. Segmentation must align with strengths the firm can realistically deliver — a firm won't go after a target market it can't reach or appeal to. Target markets are chosen where the firm's advantages matter most, and positioning highlights unique benefits competitors can't easily copy.
concepts.alt: Before choosing who to sell to, check your map (mission) and your toolkit (SWOT) — you only head where your tools can get you.

terms.def: Guide who the firm should serve and what value it promises.
Assessment of internal strengths/weaknesses and external opportunities/threats.

concepts.example: Illustrative: a small craft brewery with local roots focuses on nearby tourists rather than competing nationally with mass-market brands.

concepts.title: Step 2 — segmentation bases
concepts.explain: In Step 2 firms use segmentation bases to divide the market into groups defined by shared needs, wants and characteristics. The goal is similarity within segments (homogeneous) and clear differences between them (heterogeneous). Common bases are geographic, demographic, psychographic and behavioural. Companies often combine multiple bases (e.g., geodemographics) to build richer, more actionable customer profiles.
concepts.alt: Good segments are like well-sorted laundry piles: everything in a pile is alike, and each pile is clearly different from the others.

terms.def: Geographic, demographic, psychographic and behavioural variables used to group customers.
Members of a segment are similar; segments differ from one another.

concepts.example: Illustrative: a running-shoe company groups customers by benefit sought (speed vs comfort) and by age, combining behavioural and demographic bases.

concepts.title: Geographic segmentation
concepts.explain: Geographic segmentation groups customers by where they live — country, region, province, city, neighbourhood, urban vs rural, or climate. Location influences needs, preferences and buying habits, so demand often varies by geography. Firms can offer the same core product nationally while adjusting assortment, messaging or distribution locally. It is most useful for products whose needs vary by region.
concepts.alt: Geographic segmentation is a weather map for demand — winter boots in Winnipeg, rain gear in Vancouver.

terms.def: Grouping consumers on the basis of where they live.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Wild Lot first concentrated around Prince Edward County, then expanded through LCBO distribution across Ontario; grocers like Sobeys tailor products by neighbourhood.

concepts.title: Demographic segmentation
concepts.explain: Demographic segmentation is the most common method. It groups consumers by easily measured, objective characteristics: gender, age, ethnic group, family life-cycle stage, household type and size, income, occupation, education and religion. Census data from Statistics Canada is an excellent (and free) source of demographic segmentation data. Some groups are easiest to characterise demographically — for children's toys, age is the primary base.
concepts.alt: Demographics are the "census form" facts about a person — the boxes you'd tick on a government survey.

terms.def: Grouping consumers by objective characteristics such as age, gender, income and education.

concepts.example: Illustrative: a toy company segments mainly by children's age (e.g., toddlers vs 8–12-year-olds).

concepts.title: Psychographic segmentation
concepts.explain: Psychographic segmentation groups consumers by how they live, what they value and how they see themselves — lifestyle (e.g., VALS types such as innovators, thinkers, achievers), personality/self-concept (conservative, adventurous, health-conscious) and socio-economic status. It explains the motivations behind choices — why people buy — not just who they are or where they live. Marketers tailor offerings and messages to match these identities.
concepts.alt: Demographics tell you someone is 25; psychographics tell you they're a weekend adventurer who values sustainability.

terms.def: Segmenting by lifestyle, values, personality and self-concept.
A psychographic system grouping consumers into types such as innovators, thinkers, achievers, experiencers.
How people see themselves — 'I'm like them, so I should buy their products'.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): MEC ads appeal to self-concept; Netflix and Indigo appeal to interest-driven communities such as book lovers.

concepts.title: Behavioural segmentation
concepts.explain: Behavioural segmentation groups consumers by how they behave toward a product. The four pillars (slide notes): benefits sought (convenience, economy, prestige, quality, speed, environmental impact), usage rate (heavy, moderate, light, non-user, ex-user, potential, first-time), loyalty (not, somewhat, completely loyal), and occasion. Different motives lead different consumers to buy the same product, and firms encourage loyalty through reward programs.
concepts.alt: Behavioural segmentation looks at what people DO with a product — why they want it, how much they use it, how loyal they are and when they use it.

terms.def: Grouping consumers by benefits sought, usage rate, loyalty and occasion.
Grouping by the benefits consumers derive from a product.
Heavy, moderate, light, non-user, etc.

concepts.example: Illustrative: airline mileage and hotel points programs target loyal, frequent users.

concepts.title: Geodemographic segmentation & PRIZM
concepts.explain: Geodemographic segmentation combines geographic, demographic and lifestyle characteristics — "birds of a feather flock together". People in the same neighbourhoods (even the same postal code) tend to buy similar cars, appliances and apparel, shop at similar retailers and respond similarly to media. In Canada, PRIZM (Environics Analytics) groups neighbourhoods into 67 lifestyle clusters with descriptive names such as Urban Digerati, Mature & Secure and Keep On Trucking, making targeting practical.
concepts.alt: Geodemographics assumes your postal code says a lot about you — your neighbours probably shop the way you do.

terms.def: Combining geographic, demographic and lifestyle characteristics to segment a market.
Canadian geodemographic system that groups neighbourhoods into 67 lifestyle clusters.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): PRIZM's 'Urban Digerati' are younger, tech-savvy singles in downtown Toronto and Montreal high-rises.

concepts.title: Segment attractiveness — identifiable
concepts.explain: Step 3 evaluates segment attractiveness on four criteria: identifiable, reachable, responsive, and substantial & profitable. A segment is identifiable when the firm can tell who is in it, whether the segments are unique, and whether each segment requires a unique marketing mix. Firms must know who is in their market to design offerings for it.
concepts.alt: If you can't describe who's in a group and how they differ from others, you can't build something for them — like trying to buy a gift for a stranger.

terms.def: Evaluated by whether a segment is identifiable, reachable, responsive, and substantial & profitable.
The firm can determine who is in the segment and that it is unique and needs a distinct marketing mix.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Gap and Gap Kids target identifiable, distinct segments (adults vs kids) with different marketing mixes.

concepts.title: Segment attractiveness — reachable
concepts.explain: A segment is reachable when the firm can reach it through persuasive communications and product distribution. Consumers must know the product exists, understand what it can do for them and recognise how to buy it. The internet makes many segments easier to reach, but some areas can't be served because they aren't accessible to marketing messages or lack adequate distribution.
concepts.alt: A great message is useless if it never arrives — reachability asks "Can our ads and our products actually get to them?"

terms.def: The segment can be accessed through communications and distribution.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): La Senza must make sure any new segment can be reached, e.g., a younger audience via e-commerce.

concepts.title: Segment attractiveness — responsive
concepts.explain: A segment is responsive when its customers react similarly and positively to the firm's offering, move toward its products and accept its value proposition. Successful segmentation means choosing customers whose needs match what the firm does best — each firm succeeds by serving segments aligned with its strengths, not by chasing every opportunity. Past buyers (e.g., Gap adult customers for Gap Kids) are often the most responsive "low-hanging fruit".
concepts.alt: Responsiveness asks "Will they say yes?" — would customers believe and want this offer from this particular brand?

terms.def: Customers in the segment react positively to and accept the firm's value proposition.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slide notes): would consumers accept personal-care products like cologne from Nike? If they don't believe the value proposition, the segment isn't responsive.

concepts.title: Segment attractiveness — substantial & profitable
concepts.explain: A segment must be substantial and profitable: if it's too small or its buying power insignificant, it won't generate enough profit to support a marketing mix. Growth potential is equally important. Size in number of people is not the only consideration — a small but high-spending segment can be very profitable, and a hot segment may not last long enough to be worth the investment.
concepts.alt: Substantial & profitable asks "Is the prize big enough to be worth the trip?" — counting not just heads but dollars and future growth.

terms.def: The segment is large enough (in size and buying power) and growing enough to be worth pursuing.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): for Mark's, traditional industrial workwear is a larger, more stable segment (driven by safety rules and B2B contracts) than top-line casual apparel.

concepts.title: Segment profitability formula
concepts.explain: Segment profitability = (segment size × segment adoption % × purchase behaviour × profit margin %) − fixed costs, where purchase behaviour = purchase price × frequency of purchase. Size alone doesn't determine profitability: higher adoption and repeat purchase frequency can outweigh a smaller base, and business customers often bring larger orders, higher prices and better margins. Key factors in assessing profitability are market growth, market competitiveness and market access.
concepts.alt: Think of it as: how many people × how many of them buy × how much they spend over time × how much you keep − what it costs to play.

terms.def: (Size × adoption % × purchase behaviour × profit margin %) − fixed costs.
Purchase price × frequency of purchase.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Camillo's Lawn Service earns $140,000 from 75,000 homeowners but $600,000 from just 1,000 businesses.

concepts.title: Step 4 — select target market
concepts.explain: In Step 4 the firm selects its target market. The choice is based on a SWOT analysis that assesses the attractiveness of the opportunity and considers the organisation's competencies. The firm picks the segment(s) most responsive to its value proposition and then chooses a targeting strategy: undifferentiated, differentiated, concentrated (niche) or micromarketing.
concepts.alt: After rating every segment, you pick the ones where the opportunity is attractive AND you're good enough to win.

terms.def: The segment(s) a firm selects to pursue.
Undifferentiated, differentiated, concentrated (niche), micromarketing.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slide notes): a fashion jean line might target a young woman, while a durable work-jean line might target a male tradesperson.

concepts.title: Undifferentiated (mass) targeting
concepts.explain: An undifferentiated targeting strategy uses the same product, same message and same market. It's used when most consumers want similar benefits and works best for basic, low-involvement commodities such as salt, sugar, flour, fuel and greeting cards. Cost efficiencies come from scale rather than customisation. It's harder to sustain today because consumers expect differentiation, so even "mass" products add features, branding or convenience.
concepts.alt: Undifferentiated is one-size-fits-all — one recipe, one ad, everyone.

terms.def: Same product and message for the whole market (mass marketing).

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Esso differentiates a commodity (gasoline) through a mobile payment and loyalty app — showing even mass products now add convenience.

concepts.title: Differentiated targeting
concepts.explain: A differentiated targeting strategy gives different segments different offerings and marketing mixes, because each segment has distinct needs, interests or lifestyles. It increases total market coverage and sales opportunities and diversifies risk (weak performance in one segment is offset by others), but it brings higher costs from multiple products, campaigns and brand management.
concepts.alt: Differentiated is a restaurant with several menus — kids, vegan, date night — each designed for a different crowd.

terms.def: Targeting several segments with a different offering and marketing mix for each.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Condé Nast publishes niche magazines for different groups — The New Yorker, GQ, Vogue, Wired.

concepts.title: Concentrated (niche) targeting
concepts.explain: A concentrated (niche) targeting strategy focuses on one clearly defined segment rather than the whole market. Resources are concentrated to serve that group exceptionally well, and deep understanding of customer needs creates strong differentiation and loyalty. It's efficient for start-ups and smaller firms with limited budgets, but carries higher risk if the single segment declines or preferences change.
concepts.alt: Concentrated targeting puts all your eggs in one basket — and then watches that basket very carefully.

terms.def: Focusing on one clearly defined segment.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Newton Running targets only forefoot runners, while Nike uses a broader differentiated strategy.

concepts.title: Micromarketing (one-to-one)
concepts.explain: Micromarketing tailors products or services to individual customer needs and preferences. It creates highly personalised value and stronger relationships, and is enabled by data, AI and digital tools that track behaviour and preferences. It's more feasible online where customisation can scale, but has higher cost and complexity, so firms must balance value gained against expense.
concepts.alt: Micromarketing is the tailor-made suit of targeting — cut for one person.

terms.def: Tailoring a product or service to suit an individual customer's wants or needs.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Reebok Impact lets customers design personalised digital shoes; Mars lets shoppers personalise M&M's; Amazon customises recommendations in real time.

concepts.title: Step 5 — positioning
concepts.explain: Positioning is the mental picture — the thoughts, feelings and impressions — people have about a company, its products and brands relative to competing products, brands or companies. It is how consumers view a firm's offerings based on important attributes, placing the brand in their minds relative to competitors. Firms can position using value, product attributes, benefits and symbolism, competition, or market leadership.
concepts.alt: Positioning is the "seat" a brand occupies in your head — next to which competitors, and what label is on the seat.

terms.def: The mental picture people have of a company/product/brand relative to competitors.
Value, product attributes, benefits & symbolism, competition, market leadership.

concepts.example: Illustrative: Volvo is positioned in many consumers' minds as the 'safe' car (Ch 4 notes).

concepts.title: Positioning by value
concepts.explain: Value positioning is based on the relationship of price to quality — one of the most important considerations for consumers when they decide. Different consumers perceive value differently, so two brands can both offer "good value" to different target markets.
concepts.alt: Value = "what you get for what you pay". It doesn't mean cheapest — it means worth it, to that customer.

terms.def: Positioning on the relationship of price to quality.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): KIND bars (natural, pronounceable ingredients) and PowerBars (performance protein for athletes) both offer good value to different targets.

concepts.title: Positioning by product attributes
concepts.explain: Product-attribute positioning focuses on the attributes that are most important to the target market — e.g., innovation, quality, performance or reliability. Which attributes matter varies by target market.
concepts.alt: Attribute positioning says "Look at THIS feature" — and picks the feature your target cares about most.

terms.def: Positioning on the attributes most important to the target market.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Audi positions its all-wheel-drive Quattro on performance and handling on snowy, icy roads.

concepts.title: Positioning by benefits & symbolism
concepts.explain: This positioning emphasises the benefits of the brand as well as its psychological meaning to consumers. Well-known commercial symbols (like the Nike swoosh or the Ralph Lauren polo player) carry meaning that helps consumers differentiate a brand from competitors.
concepts.alt: Benefits & symbolism is about what the brand DOES for you and what it MEANS to you — the swoosh says more than "shoe".

terms.def: Emphasising the brand's benefits and its psychological meaning to consumers.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): SoCIAL LITE Vodka targets Gen Z on functional benefits — great taste, all natural, 80 calories, no sugar.

concepts.title: Positioning against competition
concepts.explain: Firms can position head-to-head against a specific competitor or against an entire product classification, on similar attributes within the target market. Firms that aren't the market leader often position against the leader to show they offer the same or better quality or service.
concepts.alt: Competitive positioning is a side-by-side comparison — "us versus them" — that only works if customers know who "them" is.

terms.def: Positioning against a specific competitor or an entire product classification.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Avis — 'We're number two. We try harder.' — turned second place behind Hertz into an advantage.

concepts.title: Market leadership positioning
concepts.explain: Market-leader positioning highlights a firm's dominance, scale and credibility rather than competing head-to-head. Customers often assume leaders set industry standards for quality, reliability and innovation, so leadership signals trust and lowers perceived risk. It works best for large, well-established firms with strong recognition and market share.
concepts.alt: Leadership positioning says "We're the standard" — like being the default choice everyone measures against.

terms.def: Highlighting dominance, scale and credibility as the industry leader.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Royal Bank of Canada, Loblaw, Canadian Tire, Amazon, Intel, Google and eBay.

concepts.title: Perceptual mapping
concepts.explain: A perceptual map displays, in two or more dimensions, the position of products or brands in the consumer's mind. Steps: determine consumers' perceptions and evaluations of the product in relation to competitors; identify competitors' positions; determine consumer preferences; select the position; and monitor the positioning strategy. Maps can also show the size of target markets (e.g., bigger ovals for bigger segments) to reveal gaps.
concepts.alt: A perceptual map is a "mind map" of the market — each brand is a pin on a grid of what customers care about.

terms.def: A display, in two or more dimensions, of the position of brands in consumers' minds.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): a map with sweet-vs-light taste and less-natural-vs-healthy axes places Powerade and Gatorade together (sweet, healthy) and bottled water in the light, healthy quadrant.

concepts.title: Repositioning
concepts.explain: Repositioning is a strategy in which marketers change a brand's focus to target new markets or realign the brand's core emphasis with changing market preferences. The overriding purpose is to convey that the brand meets consumers' changing needs.
concepts.alt: Repositioning is moving a brand to a new "seat" in consumers' minds — same product, new story or new audience.

terms.def: Changing a brand's focus to target new markets or realign with changing preferences.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slide notes): baking soda has been repositioned many times — new uses (fridge deodoriser, cleaning) make consumers redefine why they need it.

options: So they can adapt offerings to challenges and seize opportunities early
